<p>Therefore, as <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_i \to 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.58056em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.311664em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.04398em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>, the gradient magnitude does <strong>not</strong> decay to zero. It approaches a strict, non-zero constant <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>. The corrective outward vector remains robust regardless of how severe the collapse is.</p>
<h3 id="the-strict-purpose-of-epsilon">3. The Strict Purpose of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">ϵ</span></span></span></span></span></h3>

<p>The <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">ϵ</span></span></span></span></span> is strictly a numerical stabilizer. It ensures the denominator remains positive and differentiable, preserving the constant <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> gradient magnitude right up to the absolute limit of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<h3 id="part-7-covariance-regularization">Part 7: Covariance Regularization</h3>
<p><strong>The Threat of Informational Redundancy</strong> While the Variance term (detailed in Part 6) successfully prevents the embedding vectors from collapsing to a single zero-dimensional point, it is mathematically insufficient on its own. An encoder could still satisfy the variance threshold by mapping all data onto a 1D line in the latent space, where every dimension fluctuates identically. In this scenario, the representation suffers from informational collapse—the variables carry highly redundant information, wasting the capacity of the <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">d</span></span></span></span></span>-dimensional space.</p>
<p><strong>The Covariance Matrix</strong> To enforce that each dimension captures orthogonal, independent features, VICReg explicitly penalizes correlations between different variables within the same batch.</p>
<p>First, the empirical covariance matrix <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(Z) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.849108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; This forces the network to distribute information across the entire latent manifold, maximizing the informational content of the vectors and preventing dimensional collapse.</p>
<p><strong>The Independent Branch Advantage</strong> While the concept of decorrelation was popularized by Barlow Twins, VICReg introduces a critical mathematical distinction. Barlow Twins computes a <em>cross-correlation</em> matrix between the embeddings of the two branches, attempting to drive that matrix toward the identity.</p>
<p>VICReg, instead, computes the covariance matrix <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(Z)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">C</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mo mathvariant="normal" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(Z')</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.00189em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">C</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.751892em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">′</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> on each branch entirely independently. Furthermore, because the scale of the vectors is already controlled by VICReg’s explicit Variance hinge loss, the embeddings do not require standardization or normalization. This fundamentally protects the architecture from the numerical instabilities that occur in Barlow Twins when embeddings shrink toward zero before standardization.</p>
<p>Are you ready to move to Part 8, where we analyze the mathematical Achilles’ heel of VICReg—why computing this exact covariance matrix scales quadratically as <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(ND^2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>, creating a severe scaling bottleneck?</p>
<h3 id="part-8-computational-complexity-failures">Part 8: Computational Complexity Failures</h3>
<p><strong>The Quadratic Bottleneck of Second-Order Statistics</strong> While the covariance regularization term <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(Z)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">c</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> effectively mitigates dimensional collapse, its exact mathematical formulation introduces a fatal flaw for scaling. <p><strong>The Scaling Ceiling for Foundation Models</strong> To capture the underlying semantics of massive, complex data distributions, foundation models require vast representational capacity, meaning the expansion dimension <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span> must be exceptionally large (often <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>8192</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D \ge 8192</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.8193em; vertical-align: -0.13597em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">≥</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">8192</span></span></span></span></span> in practical VICReg setups). Furthermore, stable optimization of batch-wise statistics inherently demands large batch sizes <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>Because the complexity scales quadratically with respect to <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>, increasing the embedding capacity rapidly becomes computationally intractable on hardware. The explicit covariance objective forces a hard architectural compromise: researchers must either cripple the embedding dimension <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span> (sacrificing model expressivity) or accept prohibitive computational overhead.</p>
<p>This <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(ND^2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> wall renders explicit covariance matrix computation a dead end for frontier-scale JEPAs, requiring a fundamental shift in how target distributions are enforced.</p>
<h3 id="part-9-the-distributional-shape-gap">Part 9: The Distributional Shape Gap</h3>
<p><strong>The Limits of Second-Order Statistics</strong> Even if a model overcomes the computational hurdles of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(ND^2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> scaling, VICReg’s covariance regularization suffers from a fundamental mathematical blind spot: it only captures second-order statistics.</p>
<p>By pushing the off-diagonal elements of the covariance matrix to zero, the network successfully encourages decorrelation among the embedding dimensions. However, decorrelation does not dictate the actual geometric <em>shape</em> of the data manifold.</p>
<p><strong>The Illusion of Equivalency</strong> A distribution can perfectly match a target in its mean (first-order) and covariance (second-order) yet remain structurally entirely different from an ideal, uniform manifold. For example, a mathematically “decorrelated” representation could topologically resemble a multi-dimensional star, a hollow hypercube, or a series of disjointed clusters.</p>
<p>Because covariance constraints cannot enforce the full distributional shape of the embedding space, the resulting latent geometry is highly uncontrolled. The model satisfies the mathematical criteria of “decorrelation” while still organizing features in a way that is highly sub-optimal for generalization.</p>
<p><strong>The Need for True Isotropy</strong> For stable, information-rich training, simply ensuring that variables do not linearly covary is insufficient. The network requires true <em>isotropy</em>—meaning the distribution behaves uniformly and predictably in absolutely every direction, not just along the primary axes. Relying strictly on a covariance penalty makes it a comparatively weak proxy for this necessary geometric isotropy.</p>
<p>To build an optimal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, the objective function must abandon simple statistical metrics (like variance and covariance) and instead enforce a mathematically rigorous constraint on the <em>entire continuous distribution</em> of the latent space.</p>
<p>This sets the stage for <strong>Module 3</strong>, where we will mathematically prove exactly which target distribution JEPAs must enforce to minimize downstream risk.</p>
<h3 id="module-3-proving-the-optimal-target-geometry-—-lejepa">Module 3: Proving the Optimal Target Geometry — LeJEPA</h3>
<h3 id="part-10-downstream-risk-framework">Part 10: Downstream Risk Framework</h3>
<p><strong>The Theoretical Goal of a Foundation Model</strong></p>
<p>To definitively solve the representational shape problem outlined in Module 2, we must stop guessing which heuristic works best and instead ask a rigorous mathematical question: <em>Which exact probability distribution should the embeddings <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_\theta(x)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10764em;">f</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.10764em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">θ</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> follow to mathematically minimize empirical risk on any arbitrary, unknown downstream task?</em></p>
<p><strong>Formulating the Linear Probe</strong> The standard method for evaluating a frozen pre-trained encoder is linear probing. We can formalize this evaluation as a risk minimization problem.</p>
<p>Let <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.72243em; vertical-align: -0.0391em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span> frozen embeddings, each of dimension <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span>, produced by the encoder <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_\theta</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10764em;">f</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.10764em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">θ</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>. Let <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y \in \mathbb{R}^N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.73354em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> denote the unknown labels for a downstream task.</p>
<p>The linear probe solves a Tikhonov-regularized least-squares problem (Ridge regression) to find the optimal task parameters <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.15232em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span> is the regularization strength parameter.</p>
<p><strong>The Minimax Objective</strong> During self-supervised pre-training, the model has absolutely zero knowledge of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span></span></span></span></span>. Therefore, the mathematical objective of the JEPA is to sculpt the geometric distribution of the latent matrix <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span></span></span></span> such that the expected statistical error of the estimator <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.15232em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.95788em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.26344em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.19444em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is minimized for <em>any</em> possible realization of the target <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>To evaluate how the shape of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span></span></span></span> impacts this error, we decompose the downstream risk into two classical statistical components: <strong>Bias</strong> and <strong>Variance</strong>. By mathematically analyzing how the covariance spectrum (the eigenvalues) of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span></span></span></span> directly alters the bias and variance of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.15232em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.95788em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.26344em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.19444em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, we can derive the absolute optimal topology for the latent space.</p>
<h1 id="why-downstream-risk-becomes-the-central-problem">Why Downstream Risk Becomes the Central Problem</h1>
<p>Everything in the previous modules focused on <strong>preventing collapse</strong>.</p>
<p>We learned how to stop an encoder from producing degenerate representations by enforcing variance, decorrelation, or other regularization objectives. These methods answer an important question:</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>How do we ensure the representation contains information?</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p>However, this is only a necessary condition.</p>
<p>Once collapse has been avoided, a much deeper question remains:</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>Among all possible non-collapsed embedding spaces, which one is actually the best?</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p>This is the problem Module 3 attempts to solve.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="the-goal-of-a-foundation-model-is-fundamentally-different">The Goal of a Foundation Model Is Fundamentally Different</h1>
<p>A supervised model is trained for one specific task.</p>
<p>Given labeled pairs</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
(x_i,y_i),
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.311664em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.311664em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.03588em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mpunct">,</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>the objective is simply to minimize prediction error on those labels.</p>
<p>A foundation model operates under completely different conditions.</p>
<p>During self-supervised pretraining, the encoder only observes the raw inputs</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_N,
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="minner">…</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.328331em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>and never sees the future downstream labels</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
y.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>The encoder therefore has no knowledge of</p>
<ul>
<li>the downstream task,</li>
<li>the decision boundary,</li>
<li>the loss function,</li>
<li>or even whether the future problem is classification, regression, retrieval, or something entirely different.</li>
</ul>
<p>The only thing the encoder can control is the representation it produces,</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
z=f_\theta(x).
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10764em;">f</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.10764em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">θ</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>Consequently, the optimization problem changes completely.</p>
<p>Instead of optimizing prediction accuracy on a known task, the encoder must learn a representation that remains useful for <strong>every possible future task</strong>.</p>
<p>This shifts the objective from</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>learning one predictor</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p>to</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>learning one representation that makes every future predictor as easy as possible.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h1 id="why-we-study-frozen-representations">Why We Study Frozen Representations</h1>
<p>After pretraining, the encoder is frozen.</p>
<p>Its parameters are no longer updated.</p>
<p>Suppose the encoder maps every input into an embedding</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
z=f_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^K.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10764em;">f</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.10764em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">θ</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.891331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.891331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>These embeddings become the only information available to every downstream task.</p>
<p>The downstream learner never sees the original data directly.</p>
<p>It only receives</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_N.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.04398em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.04398em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="minner">…</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.04398em;">z</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.328331em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.04398em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>Therefore every future prediction depends entirely on how information has been organized inside this latent space.</p>
<p>If useful information has been discarded during pretraining, no downstream model can recover it.</p>
<p>Conversely, if the latent space preserves useful semantic structure, many different downstream tasks become easy to learn.</p>
<p>Thus the quality of the encoder is completely determined by the quality of its representation.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="why-linear-probing-became-the-standard-evaluation">Why Linear Probing Became the Standard Evaluation</h1>
<p>To evaluate a frozen encoder, researchers need a downstream learner.</p>
<p>In principle, this learner could be</p>
<ul>
<li>another deep neural network,</li>
<li>a transformer,</li>
<li>an MLP,</li>
<li>kernel regression,</li>
<li>nearest neighbors,</li>
<li>or any other model.</li>
</ul>
<p>However, using a powerful downstream model creates an ambiguity.</p>
<p>A strong classifier can compensate for weaknesses in the representation.</p>
<p>High downstream accuracy might simply reflect the power of the classifier rather than the quality of the embeddings.</p>
<p>To isolate the representation itself, researchers intentionally choose the simplest possible downstream model:</p>
<p>a <strong>linear classifier</strong> or <strong>linear regressor</strong>.</p>
<p>This procedure is called <strong>linear probing</strong>.</p>
<p>Only a linear mapping is allowed to learn.</p>
<p>The encoder remains completely frozen.</p>
<p>If a simple linear model can already solve many tasks, then the representation must already organize the data into a useful geometric structure.</p>
<p>Linear probing therefore measures</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>How linearly accessible is the information stored inside the representation?</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p>It does <strong>not</strong> measure the absolute capability of the encoder.</p>
<p>Rather, it measures how much additional computation is required to extract the information already present in the latent space.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="why-we-use-ridge-regression">Why We Use Ridge Regression</h1>
<p>Suppose the encoder produces the embedding matrix</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup><mo separator="true">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Z\in\mathbb R^{N\times K},
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.72243em; vertical-align: -0.0391em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.08577em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.891331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mbin mtight">×</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>where</p>
<ul>
<li>(N) is the number of samples,</li>
<li>(K) is the embedding dimension.</li>
</ul>
<p>Suppose the downstream task has unknown targets</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
y\in\mathbb R^N.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.73354em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.891331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.891331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>A linear probe assumes that these targets can be approximated by</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>Z</mi><mi>β</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\hat y=Z\beta,
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.69444em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.19444em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.19444em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">Zβ</span><span class="mpunct">,</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>where</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\beta\in\mathbb R^K
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.891331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.891331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>contains the learnable linear coefficients.</p>
<p>The simplest objective is ordinary least squares,</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo></mrow><mi>β</mi></munder><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>Z</mi><mi>β</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\min_\beta \|y-Z\beta\|^2.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.63822em; vertical-align: -0.888216em;"></span><span class="mop op-limits"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.66786em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.34789em; margin-left: 0em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span></span></span><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class=""><span class="mop">min</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.888216em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">−</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.11411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">Zβ</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.864108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>This asks a straightforward question:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Which linear combination of the embedding coordinates best predicts the labels?</p>
</blockquote>
<p>In practice, however, many embedding dimensions may be highly correlated or noisy.</p>
<p>Direct least squares can therefore become unstable.</p>
<p>To stabilize the solution, we penalize excessively large coefficients,</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mi>β</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo separator="true">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\lambda\|\beta\|^2,
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.11411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.864108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>leading to Ridge regression,</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>arg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><munder><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo></mrow><mi>β</mi></munder><mrow><mo fence="true">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>Z</mi><mi>β</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mi>β</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∥</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo fence="true">)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \hat{\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left( \Vert y - Z\beta \Vert^2 + \lambda \Vert \beta \Vert^2 \right). </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.15232em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.95788em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.26344em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.19444em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.75232em; vertical-align: -0.888216em;"></span><span class="mop">ar<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mop op-limits"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.66786em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.34789em; margin-left: 0em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span></span></span></span><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class=""><span class="mop">min</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.888216em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="minner"><span class="mopen delimcenter" style="top: 0em;"><span class="delimsizing size1">(</span></span><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">y</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">−</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">Zβ</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.864108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05278em;">β</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">∥</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.864108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose delimcenter" style="top: 0em;"><span class="delimsizing size1">)</span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>The additional regularization discourages the probe from relying too heavily on any single embedding direction and guarantees a unique solution even when the embedding matrix is poorly conditioned.</p>
<p>This is why Ridge regression is the standard mathematical model analyzed throughout the remainder of the chapter.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="why-representation-geometry-suddenly-matters">Why Representation Geometry Suddenly Matters</h1>
<p>Notice something important.</p>
<p>Once the encoder is frozen,</p>
<p>the downstream learner has only one object available:</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
Z.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>Nothing else from pretraining survives.</p>
<p>The downstream task therefore depends entirely on the <strong>geometry</strong> of the embedding matrix.</p>
<p>Intuitively, imagine every embedding as a point in a high-dimensional space.</p>
<p>Together they form a geometric cloud.</p>
<p>Different encoders may produce clouds with completely different shapes.</p>
<p>For example,</p>
<ul>
<li>one cloud may spread uniformly in every direction,</li>
<li>another may stretch into a long thin ellipsoid,</li>
<li>another may collapse near a lower-dimensional plane,</li>
<li>another may separate into disconnected clusters.</li>
</ul>
<p>Although all of these representations may avoid complete collapse, they do <strong>not</strong> provide the same geometry for downstream learning.</p>
<p>The shape of this cloud determines how easily future tasks can separate different samples.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="covariance-describes-the-shape-of-the-embedding-cloud">Covariance Describes The Shape Of The Embedding Cloud</h1>
<p>To study this geometry mathematically, we compute the covariance matrix,</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
C(Z).
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">C</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mord">.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>The covariance matrix summarizes how the embedding coordinates vary together across the dataset.</p>
<p>Its eigenvectors define the principal directions of variation.</p>
<p>Its eigenvalues measure how much information lies along each of those directions.</p>
<p>Large eigenvalues correspond to directions where the data varies substantially.</p>
<p>Small eigenvalues correspond to directions where almost no variation exists.</p>
<p>One can think of the eigenvalues as describing how “wide” or “narrow” the embedding cloud is in every direction.</p>
<p>If every eigenvalue is identical, the cloud spreads equally in every direction.</p>
<p>If some eigenvalues are much larger than others, the cloud becomes elongated, indicating that most information has been concentrated into only a few directions.</p>
<p>This property is called <strong>anisotropy</strong>.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="why-bias-and-variance-suddenly-become-the-focus">Why Bias And Variance Suddenly Become The Focus</h1>
<p>The remaining question is no longer</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Does the representation contain information?</p>
</blockquote>
<p>Instead it becomes</p>
<blockquote>
<p>How does the geometry of the representation affect the quality of future predictors?</p>
</blockquote>
<p>For linear estimators, statistical learning theory provides a natural answer.</p>
<p>The prediction error can be decomposed into two fundamental components:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Bias</strong>, measuring systematic error introduced by the estimator.</li>
<li><strong>Variance</strong>, measuring how sensitive the estimator is to changes in the training data.</li>
</ul>
<p>Every linear estimator ultimately trades these two quantities against one another.</p>
<p>Therefore, if the geometry of the embedding space changes either bias or variance, it directly changes downstream prediction performance.</p>
<p>This makes bias and variance the natural quantities to study.</p>
<p>Importantly, this does <strong>not</strong> mean they explain every possible machine learning algorithm.</p>
<p>They characterize the behavior of the particular downstream estimator being analyzed—in this case, a linear probe.</p>
<p>The goal of the following sections is therefore very specific:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>Determine how the covariance spectrum (its eigenvalues) influences the bias and variance of a linear estimator.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>If one geometric arrangement always produces lower bias and lower variance than another, then that geometry is mathematically preferable for linear downstream tasks.</p>
<p>Only after establishing this result does the analysis later generalize beyond linear probes to non-linear estimators such as <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03148em;">k</span></span></span></span></span>-Nearest Neighbors and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression.</p>
<p>Thus, the progression of Module 3 is deliberate:</p>
<ol>
<li>Freeze the encoder.</li>
<li>Study the simplest downstream learner (a linear probe).</li>
<li>Analyze how representation geometry affects its statistical error.</li>
<li>Identify the geometric properties that minimize that error.</li>
<li>Later, investigate whether the same conclusions continue to hold for more expressive non-linear predictors.</li>
</ol>
<p>The remainder of the module is devoted to answering this question rigorously.</p>
<h3 id="part-11-anisotropy-bias--variance">Part 11: Anisotropy Bias &amp; Variance</h3>

<strong>Conclusion:</strong> Squeezing information into an anisotropic geometry creates an unstable estimator that varies wildly across different training sets.</p>
<p>By proving that anisotropy strictly inflates both bias and variance under linear regimes, the mathematical mandate becomes clear: the embedding distribution <em>must</em> be isotropic.</p>
<p>Are you ready for Part 12, where we discard the assumption of a linear probe and push this geometric optimality proof into the non-linear realm using <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03148em;">k</span></span></span></span></span>-NN and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regressors?</p>
<p>Part 11 in detail:</p>
<h1 id="why-we-compare-two-geometries">Why We Compare Two Geometries</h1>
<p>In Part 10, we established that the encoder cannot optimize for any specific downstream task because those tasks are unknown during self-supervised pretraining.</p>
<p>Instead, the only object the encoder can control is the geometry of its embedding space.</p>
<p>The next question therefore becomes</p>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>If two embedding spaces contain the same semantic information, can one geometric arrangement still be mathematically better than the other?</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p>This is the central question of Part 11.</p>
<p>Notice that we are <strong>not</strong> comparing two different encoders that learned different features.</p>
<p>Instead, we imagine an idealized thought experiment.</p>
<p>Both encoders have learned exactly the same semantics.</p>
<p>Both preserve exactly the same information.</p>
<p>The only difference is <strong>how that information is distributed throughout the latent space.</strong></p>
<p>This allows us to isolate the effect of geometry alone.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="holding-everything-else-constant">Holding Everything Else Constant</h1>
<p>Whenever we compare two systems mathematically, we must ensure that only one variable changes.</p>
<p>Otherwise, we cannot determine which difference caused the observed behavior.</p>
<p>Suppose one embedding has larger total variance simply because it contains more information.</p>
<p>If it performs better, we cannot conclude that its geometry is responsible.</p>
<p>Perhaps it simply learned richer features.</p>
<p>Therefore Part 11 imposes two constraints.</p>
<p>Both embedding spaces</p>
<ul>
<li>encode the same intrinsic semantic information,</li>
<li>possess the same total variance (sometimes called the same total energy).</li>
</ul>
<p>The only thing allowed to change is <strong>how that total variance is distributed across different directions.</strong></p>
<p>This creates a fair comparison.</p>
<hr>
<h1 id="the-meaning-of-total-variance">The Meaning Of Total Variance</h1>
<p>Suppose the covariance matrix of the embeddings is</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\Sigma.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">Σ.</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>Its eigenvalues are</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">.</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">
\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_K.
</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; <p>The total variance is simply</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">tr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_k</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em;
