margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.05724em;">j</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">ϵ</span><span class="mclose">))</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p>As analyzed in Part 6, VICReg’s variance hinge loss forces the embeddings to spread out along each axis so that the standard deviation meets a target threshold <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05556em;">γ</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>However, <strong>variance is a second-order global statistic</strong>. A network can trivially satisfy a large global variance threshold <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05556em;">γ</span></span></span></span></span> while simultaneously creating a latent space with a massive Fisher Information <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>For example, an encoder could satisfy the variance constraint by mapping embeddings into:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Multiple disjoint, ultra-dense 0-dimensional points</strong> far apart from each other.</li>
<li><strong>A thin, hollow <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span>-dimensional shell or star shape</strong>.</li>
</ol>
<p>Both configurations possess high variance (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Var</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Var}(Z) \ge \gamma</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">Var</span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">≥</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.05556em;">γ</span></span></span></span></span>), but both feature infinite local density gradients (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla p(x) \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∇</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">∞</span></span></span></span></span>) at the boundaries, causing <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p) \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">∞</span></span></span></span></span>. This phenomenon was defined in Part 9 as the <strong>Distributional Shape Gap</strong>.</p>
<hr>
<h2 id="iv.-summary-of-the-fisher-bottleneck-principle">IV. Summary of the Fisher Bottleneck Principle</h2>
<ol>
<li>
<p><strong>Local Non-Linear Risk depends on Latent Smoothness:</strong> Non-linear estimators (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.03148em;">k</span></span></span></span></span>-NN, kernel probes) perform spatial averaging around query points. Unsmooth latent densities corrupt this spatial averaging by skewing neighbor distributions toward high-density peaks.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong><span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> Quantifies Latent Roughness:</strong> The Fisher Information Functional <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> mathematically measures the integrated squared roughness (score energy) of the embedding space.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>The Core Mandate:</strong> Minimizing downstream risk on arbitrary unknown tasks requires minimizing <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> under a fixed scale constraint.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>This establishes the theoretical foundation for the rest of the JEPA curriculum: <strong>How do we design a loss function that explicitly forces <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> to its theoretical minimum?</strong></p>
<hr>
<h3 id="part-13-isotropic-gaussian-proof">Part 13: Isotropic Gaussian Proof</h3>
<p><strong>The Fisher Information Bound</strong> As established in Part 12, minimizing downstream risk for non-linear probes mathematically reduces to minimizing the Fisher Information functional <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> of the embedding density <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>For any mean-zero probability density <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span></span> on <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> with covariance <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>X</mi><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma = \mathbb{E}[XX^T] &gt; 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.09133em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathbb">E</span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">X</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">X</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">]</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">&gt;</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>, the Fisher Information functional <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> satisfies a fundamental bound derived from the matrix Cramér-Rao inequality. Taking the trace of this bound yields the following strict inequality: <span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> J(p) \ge \text{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}) </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">≥</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.11411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">tr</span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.864108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.113em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span></span></p>
<p><strong>The Gaussian Equality</strong> The exact minimum of this bound—where <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p) = \text{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord text"><span class="mord">tr</span></span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>—is mathematically achieved if and only if the score function <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla \log p(x)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∇</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mop">lo<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> is a strictly affine function of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>Integrating this score function identity proves that <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span></span> must be a Gaussian distribution with precision matrix <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>. Therefore, for any arbitrarily fixed covariance <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">Σ</span></span></span></span></span>, the Gaussian <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.14736em;">N</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> is the unique absolute minimizer of the Fisher Information.</p>
<p><strong>The Isotropic Scalar Constraint</strong> The final mathematical step is to find which specific Gaussian geometry minimizes the trace of the precision matrix, <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mtext>tr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{1}{\lambda_k}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; <p><strong>The Absolute Optimum</strong> Combining these two proofs locks in the theoretical target:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p>The Gaussian uniquely minimizes <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.09618em;">J</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> for a given covariance.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>An Isotropic covariance (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma = sI_K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">Σ</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">I</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.328331em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.07847em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>) uniquely minimizes the trace constraint.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Thus, the Isotropic Gaussian distribution (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0, sI_K)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; margin-left: -0.07847em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>) uniquely minimizes the Fisher Information functional <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(p)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; Consequently, forcing JEPA embeddings to perfectly match an Isotropic Gaussian is the mathematically guaranteed strategy to minimize worst-case prediction risk on any unknown downstream task.</p>
<h3 id="module-4-distribution-sketching-via-characteristic-functions-—-sigreg">Module 4: Distribution Sketching via Characteristic Functions — SIGReg</h3>
<h3 id="part-14-hyperspherical-cramér-wold-theorem">Part 14: Hyperspherical Cramér-Wold Theorem</h3>
<p><strong>The Dimensionality Trap of Density Matching</strong> Part 13 established that the mathematically optimal embedding distribution is an Isotropic Gaussian. However, directly matching two probability distributions <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_\theta</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">8192</span></span></span></span></span>) is computationally intractable. Traditional multivariate statistical tests suffer from the curse of dimensionality, exhibiting at least quadratic complexity with respect to the number of samples, making them impossible to integrate into a standard neural network training loop.</p>
<p>To bypass this <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N^2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; <p><strong>The Hyperspherical Cramér-Wold Theorem</strong> The mathematical vehicle that permits this dimensional reduction is the Cramér-Wold theorem. It states that a high-dimensional probability measure is uniquely and entirely determined by its one-dimensional projections.</p>
<p>Let <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">X</span></span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.22222em;">Y</span></span></span></span></span> be <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>-valued random vectors. The Hyperspherical Cramér-Wold theorem asserts that their multivariate distributions are identical if and only if their 1D projections along every possible unit vector <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u \in \mathbb{S}^{K-1}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.5782em; <p><strong>The Target Reduction:</strong> Because the global target <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.87777em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span></span></span></span></span> is an Isotropic Gaussian, any 1D projection of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.87777em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span></span></span></span></span> along any unit vector <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">a</span></span></span></span></span> is mathematically guaranteed to be a standard 1D Gaussian.</p>

<li>

<p>By aggregating these univariate test statistics over <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">M</span></span></span></span></span> random directions, the network “sketches” the high-dimensional space. This transforms the computationally impossible task of high-dimensional density matching into a highly parallelizable series of 1D comparisons.</p>
<p>The next mathematical decision is determining exactly <em>which</em> univariate statistical test to apply to these 1D projections, which leads directly into Part 15 and the evaluation of empirical characteristic functions.</p>
<h3 id="part-15-empirical-characteristic-functions-ecfs">Part 15: Empirical Characteristic Functions (ECFs)</h3>
<p><strong>The Univariate Test Selection Problem</strong> With the high-dimensional geometry reduced to a series of 1D random projections (Part 14), the architecture must now select a univariate statistical test to measure the deviation between the empirical 1D slices and the target 1D standard Gaussian. The choice of this test dictates whether gradient-based training will succeed or catastrophically fail.</p>
<p>Classical statistical tests fall into three primary families, but only one survives the rigorous mathematical and computational demands of deep learning.</p>
<p><strong>1. The Failure of Moments (Jarque-Bera)</strong> Moment-based tests attempt to match the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis of the distributions.</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>The Identifiability Issue:</strong> A finite set of moments mathematically cannot uniquely identify a probability distribution. The network can easily find degenerate shortcut solutions that perfectly match the first four moments but look nothing like a Gaussian.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Exploding Gradients:</strong> To guarantee uniqueness, the test would need to evaluate infinitely high moments. However, sample-gradients of moments are polynomial; minimizing higher-order moments causes the gradients to explode, destroying training stability.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>2. The Impracticality of Cumulative Density Functions (CDFs)</strong> CDF-based tests, such as the Cramér-von Mises or Anderson-Darling tests, measure the integral of the squared difference between the empirical CDF and the target CDF.</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>The Sorting Bottleneck:</strong> Computing an empirical CDF strictly requires sorting the data. Sorting has an algorithmic complexity of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N \log N)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mop">lo<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> and is fundamentally a non-differentiable operation, requiring complex continuous relaxations to pass gradients.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Distributed Parallelization Collapse:</strong> Sorting breaks the embarrassingly parallel nature of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). In multi-GPU setups (Distributed Data Parallel), sorting demands heavy synchronization across devices, severely throttling training speed.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>3. The Fourier-Domain Solution: Empirical Characteristic Functions (ECFs)</strong> To overcome the instabilities of moments and the sorting bottlenecks of CDFs, the mathematical solution is to shift the density matching into the Fourier domain using the Empirical Characteristic Function (ECF).</p>
<p>The Characteristic Function is the exact Fourier transform of the probability density function. For a set of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.0714286em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.5em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size3 size1 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">n</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.143em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> This mathematical shift unlocks three absolute advantages for deep learning:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p><strong>Differentiability:</strong> The complex exponential is naturally and smoothly differentiable everywhere.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Scalability:</strong> Computing the ECF requires zero sorting. Because it is a simple arithmetic average of independent exponentials, it scales with strictly linear <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> complexity. Furthermore, it is perfectly suited for multi-GPU training, as the average can be seamlessly synchronized across devices using a highly efficient <code>all_reduce</code> operation.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Identifiability:</strong> Unlike finite moments, the Characteristic Function uniquely and entirely defines the probability distribution.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>By operating in the Fourier domain, the JEPA can mathematically enforce the target density efficiently and smoothly. The exact mechanism of evaluating this ECF difference leads directly to the Epps-Pulley test in Part 16.</p>
<h3 id="part-16-the-epps-pulley-test">Part 16: The Epps-Pulley Test</h3>
<p><strong>The Fourier-Domain Metric</strong> Building directly upon the Empirical Characteristic Function (ECF) established in Part 15, the Epps-Pulley test provides the exact mathematical metric to evaluate the distance between the empirical 1D slices and the standard Gaussian target.</p>
<p>The test calculates the squared <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.84444em; <p><strong>The Mathematical Formulation of Fourier Distance</strong> With the empirical distribution mapped into the Fourier domain via the Empirical Characteristic Function (ECF) <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>X</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\phi}_X(t)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.20788em; <p>While tests like Kolmogorov-Smirnov rely on the <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_\infty</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.84444em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.01968em;">l</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.151392em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.01968em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">∞</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>-norm (evaluating the single maximum difference between distributions), they produce extremely sparse gradients that are disastrous for deep learning optimization. The mathematical solution is the Epps-Pulley test, which computes the weighted <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.84444em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.01968em;">l</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.01968em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>-norm difference across the continuous frequency spectrum.</p>

vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.13889em;">EP</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 2.38457em; <p><strong>The Role of the Weighting Function</strong> The integral includes a specific Gaussian weighting function, typically defined as <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(t) = e^{-t^2/\alpha^2}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; This weight acts as a fundamental mathematical filter:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>It places maximum emphasis on the low frequencies (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.61508em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span></span></span></span></span> near <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>), ensuring the network correctly matches the macroscopic topological features—the mean, variance, and broad shape of the distribution.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>It aggressively decays at high frequencies, suppressing microscopic empirical noise and preventing the network from overfitting to individual batch sampling artifacts.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Theorem 4: The Guarantee of Absolute Stability</strong> The defining mathematical property that elevates the Epps-Pulley test above all other distribution-matching candidates is its provable absolute stability. Because the magnitude of a complex exponential is always bounded (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|e^{itX}| = 1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.09133em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∣</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">e</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">tX</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">∣</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span></span>), the ECF and its derivatives are strictly bounded for <em>any</em> input distribution.</p>

Therefore, regardless of how severely degenerate, skewed, or collapsed the initial empirical distribution becomes, the gradient backpropagating through the encoder is mathematically incapable of exploding.</p>
<p><strong>Tractable Integration</strong> In practice, evaluating the infinite integral analytically is not required. The Epps-Pulley test can be executed via a highly efficient numerical approximation using the trapezoidal quadrature rule. Because the Characteristic Function is highly accurate near zero and decays predictably, the integral converges reliably with as few as 17 deterministic integration knots over a finite domain (e.g., <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-5, 5]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">−</span><span class="mord">5</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord">5</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span></span>).</p>
<p>By embedding the Epps-Pulley test into the sketching framework, the architecture achieves a stable, bounded, and differentiable distance metric. In Part 17, we will assemble these pieces into the complete SIGReg algorithm, proving its ultimate linear complexity.</p>
<h3 id="part-17-sigreg-algorithmic-architecture">Part 17: SIGReg Algorithmic Architecture</h3>
<p><strong>The Linear Complexity Breakthrough</strong> By shifting from the exact multivariate covariance matrix (VICReg) to 1D sketching via characteristic functions (Module 4), Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) fundamentally dismantles the quadratic <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><msup><mi>D</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(ND^2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> scaling bottleneck.</p>
<p>The mathematical execution of the SIGReg algorithm operates through a strict sequence of highly parallelizable matrix operations:</p>

<p><strong>4. The Objective Evaluation</strong> The final distance is calculated by squaring the absolute difference between the aggregated empirical ECF and the theoretical standard Gaussian CF (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\exp(-t^2/2)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.06411em; The trapezoidal rule approximates the integral across the <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">M</span></span></span></span></span> slices, yielding a scalar loss value.</p>
<p><strong>The Complexity Triumvirate</strong> The absolute algorithmic complexity of SIGReg scales linearly with respect to all primary dimensions: batch size (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span>), embedding dimension (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>), and the number of slices (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">M</span></span></span></span></span>).</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Time Complexity:</strong> <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>M</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NDM + N M T_{knots})</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">M</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; </li>
<li>

<p>However, despite providing a scalable, mathematically provable mechanism for targeting the Isotropic Gaussian, SIGReg harbors a deep, fatal flaw in its optimization dynamics when the features enter a collapsed state.</p>
<p>Are you ready to move to Part 18, where we mathematically expose the Scale-Shape Coupling Problem that breaks SIGReg’s gradient behavior?</p>
<h3 id="part-18-the-scale-shape-coupling-problem">Part 18: The Scale-Shape Coupling Problem</h3>
<p><strong>The Monolithic Target</strong></p>
<p>While SIGReg elegantly solves the computational bottleneck of high-dimensional density matching via 1D slicing, it introduces a severe structural flaw by utilizing a monolithic optimization target.</p>
<p>By applying the Epps-Pulley test to match empirical projections directly to a standard normal distribution <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.14736em;">N</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>, SIGReg forces the network to simultaneously optimize two fundamentally distinct geometric properties within a single mathematical objective:</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p><strong>Scale:</strong> The spread or magnitude of the embeddings (enforcing a variance of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span></span>).</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Shape:</strong> The actual morphological distribution of the data (enforcing the Gaussian bell curve).</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>The Brittleness of Coupling</strong> Fusing scale and shape into one inseparable metric strips the architecture of its flexibility across different data regimes. If a dataset is noisy, sparse, or long-tailed, the network might need a relaxed shape constraint but a strict scale constraint to prevent collapse. Because SIGReg does not decouple these properties, the researcher cannot reweight the objectives, limiting the architecture’s capacity to handle low-quality or out-of-distribution (OOD) data.</p>
<p><strong>The Gradient Vanishing Act</strong></p>
<p>The absolute fatal flaw of this coupled approach reveals itself when the network begins to fail.</p>
<p>If the prediction loss temporarily overpowers the regularization, the encoder’s embeddings will begin to shrink, initiating topological collapse. As the feature norm approaches zero, the empirical distribution effectively collapses into a Dirac delta function at the origin.</p>
<p>Mathematical simulations of the Epps-Pulley test under these collapse conditions demonstrate a catastrophic failure: <strong>as the feature scale shrinks, the magnitude of the gradient <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\nabla L||</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∣∣∇</span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="mord">∣∣</span></span></span></span></span> generated by SIGReg exponentially diminishes</strong>.</p>
<p><strong>The Fatal Irony</strong> This creates a paradoxical optimization trap. The primary purpose of a regularizer in a JEPA is to act as a repulsive force to pull the network <em>out</em> of a collapsed state. However, because SIGReg’s gradient dies as the spatial scale collapses, the corrective signal vanishes precisely when the network needs it the most. The architecture becomes locked in the degenerate shortcut, entirely unable to recover.</p>
<p>To rescue the sketching paradigm from this gradient death spiral, the architecture must completely sever the mathematical link between scale and shape.</p>
<p>Are you ready for Part 19, where we fully deconstruct the vanishing gradient profile of SIGReg and set up the foundation for optimal transport?</p>
<h3 id="part-19-the-catastrophic-bottleneck">Part 19: The Catastrophic Bottleneck</h3>

<p>As <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_n \to 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.58056em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.151392em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">n</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>, this partial derivative does not provide a strong outward directional vector; instead, the geometric relationship between the empirical points and the target distribution becomes completely blurred in the Fourier domain.</p>
<p><strong>Empirical Proof of the Dead Zone</strong> This mathematical property manifests as a catastrophic decay in gradient magnitude. As the embedding collapses and <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">4</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>), the gradient magnitude of SIGReg exponentially decays toward <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; <p>The Epps-Pulley test essentially becomes “blind” at the origin. The repulsive force vanishes entirely precisely when the network requires the strongest possible corrective signal to push the embeddings back out into the latent space.</p>
<p><strong>The Paradigm Shift</strong> To resolve this, the architecture requires a mathematical metric that maintains a constant, robust gradient magnitude <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\nabla L||</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∣∣∇</span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="mord">∣∣</span></span></span></span></span> even when <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r \to 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>. The metric must possess a geometric awareness of distance that characteristic functions lack.</p>
<p>If a point mass is at the origin and the target is a standard Gaussian, the gradient should point outward with a magnitude proportional to the necessary physical displacement, regardless of how small the current variance is. This requirement forces the final architectural evolution: abandoning the Fourier domain and entering the realm of Optimal Transport.</p>
<h3 id="module-5-optimal-transport--decoupled-regularization-—-visreg">Module 5: Optimal Transport &amp; Decoupled Regularization — VISReg</h3>
<h3 id="part-20-the-principle-of-decoupling">Part 20: The Principle of Decoupling</h3>
<p><strong>Dismantling the Monolithic Target</strong> To escape the vanishing gradient trap of SIGReg, the architecture must abandon the attempt to match both the volume and the geometry of a distribution simultaneously. Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) achieves this by strictly partitioning the monolithic Isotropic Gaussian target into two completely independent mathematical objectives: Scale and Shape.</p>
<p>By decoupling these properties, the architecture regains the flexibility to control the embedding magnitude independently from its topological structure, a critical advantage for handling sparse or low-quality data regimes.</p>
<p><strong>The Scale Objective: Resurrecting the Repulsive Force</strong> To guarantee that the network possesses a permanent escape velocity from complete collapse, VISReg resurrects the variance hinge loss from VICReg. Let <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.98587em; vertical-align: -0.0391em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.94677em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.25233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mbin mtight">×</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> denote the batch of mean-centered embeddings. <p>Because this loss relies purely on the first-order distance to a target variance (rather than a characteristic function evaluated near zero), its gradient mathematically approaches a constant value during collapse. This ensures an unrelenting, reliable corrective signal when the feature scale <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r \to 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p><strong>Isolating Shape: The Mathematical Role of the Stop-Gradient</strong> To optimize the actual geometric shape of the manifold, the architecture must evaluate the embeddings independent of their current magnitude. This requires normalizing the centered embeddings. However, if this normalization is fully differentiable, the gradients from the shape matching objective will backpropagate through the variance term, causing destructive interference.</p>

<p><strong>Heuristic vs. Principled Operations</strong> This marks a profound shift in the taxonomy of self-supervised mechanics. In earlier asymmetric architectures (like BYOL or SimSiam), the stop-gradient was deployed as an opaque collapse-prevention heuristic to break gradient symmetry between a teacher and student.</p>
<p>In VISReg, the stop-gradient serves a strictly principled role: absolute objective decomposition. It mathematically severs shape optimization from scale optimization, ensuring that the shape gradients optimize purely for latent topology while the scale gradients independently dictate spatial volume.</p>
<p>With the scale secured and the normalized vectors <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Z}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.92019em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.92019em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.60233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">~</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> isolated, the architecture requires a new metric to sketch the target shape—one that does not suffer from the Fourier domain’s vanishing gradient problem. This forces the introduction of Optimal Transport, which we will mathematically define in Part 21.</p>
<h3 id="part-21-1d-optimal-transport-theory">Part 21: 1D Optimal Transport Theory</h3>
<p><strong>The Optimal Transport Alternative</strong><br>
To overcome the “blind spot” of characteristic functions near the origin, the mathematical framework must transition from measuring frequency-domain discrepancies to measuring spatial “work.” Optimal Transport (OT) provides this exact mechanism.</p>
<p>The Wasserstein distance (derived from OT) measures the minimum cost required to physically warp one probability distribution into another. Unlike the Epps-Pulley test, the Wasserstein distance evaluates the geometric displacement between point masses. If an empirical distribution collapses toward zero while the target is a standard Gaussian, the Wasserstein gradient does not vanish; it points directly outward with a magnitude proportional to the spatial displacement required to fix the collapse.</p>
<p><strong>The Computational Intractability of Multivariate OT</strong><br>
The fatal drawback of Optimal Transport is its algorithmic complexity. Computing the exact <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; This is computationally catastrophic for deep learning and absolutely impossible to run at every step of a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture.</p>
<p><strong>The 1D Mathematical Miracle</strong><br>
However, a profound mathematical exception exists in exactly one dimension. Because the real line <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68889em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathbb">R</span></span></span></span></span> is strictly ordered, the optimal transport plan between two 1D distributions is strictly monotonic. You do not need to solve a complex linear programming problem to find which point should move where; you simply align the points in order from smallest to largest.</p>
<p><strong>Lemma 3.2: 1D Wasserstein Closed-Form</strong><br>
This strict ordering yields a highly efficient closed-form solution.
