This provides a shape-matching objective that is deterministic, strictly differentiable, geometrically aware, and requires only an <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N \log N)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mop">lo<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> 1D sorting operation.</p>
<p>This optimal 1D metric provides the absolute foundation for the Sliced-Wasserstein sketching mechanism that defines VISReg.</p>
<h3 id="part-22-sliced-wasserstein-sketching">Part 22: Sliced Wasserstein Sketching</h3>
<p><strong>Fusing OT with Cramér-Wold Projections</strong><br>
To project the robust, non-vanishing optimal transport gradients (Part 21) into the high-dimensional latent space (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>), the architecture re-engages the Hyperspherical Cramér-Wold Theorem (Part 14). By computing the 1D 2-Wasserstein distance (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}_2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.08222em;">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.08222em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>) across a set of random 1D projections, the network constructs the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD).</p>
<p><strong>The Sketching Algorithm</strong><br>
The mathematical execution of Sliced Wasserstein sketching operates on the explicitly normalized and stop-gradient-isolated embeddings <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.95929em; <p><strong>The Ultimate Shape Enforcement</strong><br>
Unlike the VICReg covariance constraint, which captures only second-order decorrelation, the Sliced Wasserstein target enforces the absolute, full marginal distribution along every single projected direction. It mathematically coerces the topological shape of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Z}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.92019em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.92019em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.60233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">~</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> into an Isotropic Gaussian without suffering from the vanishing gradients of the Fourier domain.</p>
<hr>
<p>Are you ready to advance to Part 23, where we assemble the full mathematical framework of VISReg by synthesizing this shape sketching with the scale constraints?</p>
<h3 id="part-23-visreg-loss-formulation">Part 23: VISReg Loss Formulation</h3>
<p><strong>The Tripartite Regularization</strong><br>
With the scale and shape mathematically decoupled, the Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) architecture defines its total regularization objective, <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{Reg}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.969438em; vertical-align: -0.286108em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.328331em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.00773em;">R</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">g</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.286108em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, by combining three distinct terms.</p>
<p><strong>1. The Scale Constraint (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{scale}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">sc</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">a</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.01968em;">l</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>)</strong><br>
Operating on the centered embeddings <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.98587em; vertical-align: -0.0391em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.94677em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.25233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">^</span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">∈</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.841331em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathbb">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.841331em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mbin mtight">×</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, the variance loss guarantees the physical volume of the latent space does not collapse:<br>
<span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>D</mi></mfrac><mo>∑</mo><mo>∗</mo><msup><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>D</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \mathcal{L}*{scale} = \frac{1}{D} \sum*{j=1}^D (1 - \sigma_j(\hat{Z}))^2 </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; <p><strong>2. The Shape Constraint (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{shape}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.969438em; vertical-align: -0.286108em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">s</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">ha</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">p</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.286108em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>)</strong><br>

<span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>∑</mo><mo>∗</mo><msup><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mtext>sort</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \mathcal{L}*{shape} = \frac{1}{K} \sum*{k=1}^K ||\text{sort}(\tilde{Z}w_k) - q_N||_2^2 </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; <p><strong>3. The Center Constraint (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{center}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">ce</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">n</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">er</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>)</strong><br>
To further increase training robustness, VISReg incorporates a simple centering loss on the batch mean <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.625em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">μ</span></span></span></span></span>. This prevents the entire embedding manifold from drifting aimlessly through the high-dimensional space:<br>
<span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \mathcal{L}_{center} = ||\mu||_2^2 </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; <p><strong>The Total Regularization Objective</strong><br>
These three components are weighted by their respective hyperparameters to form the complete regularization loss:<br>
<span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \mathcal{L}*{Reg} = \lambda*{scale}\mathcal{L}*{scale} + \lambda*{shape}\mathcal{L}*{shape} + \lambda*{center}\mathcal{L}*{center} </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; <h3 id="part-24-collapse-escape-dynamics">Part 24: Collapse Escape Dynamics</h3>
<p><strong>The Mathematical Guarantee of Recovery</strong><br>
The ultimate test of any self-supervised regularization scheme is how it behaves when the network is pushed to the absolute brink of topological collapse. In Part 19, we established that frequency-based sketching methods (like SIGReg’s Epps-Pulley test) suffer a catastrophic failure: their gradient magnitude <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\nabla L||</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∣∣∇</span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="mord">∣∣</span></span></span></span></span> decays exponentially as the feature scale <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span></span></span></span></span> shrinks, vanishing completely in the collapse region.</p>
<p>Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) fundamentally solves this optimization trap through the mathematical design of its decoupled scale objective.</p>

This mathematical formulation guarantees that as the embedding collapses, the gradient does not vanish; instead, it approaches a strict, non-zero constant.</p>
<p><strong>The Stop-Gradient Shield</strong><br>
If the shape objective (the Sliced Wasserstein Distance) were allowed to backpropagate freely through the variance calculation, it could generate destructive interference that mathematically neutralizes this constant outward force.</p>
<p>This is exactly why the stop-gradient operator in the normalization step (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Z} = \frac{\hat{Z}}{sg(\sigma) + \epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.92019em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.92019em;"><span class="" style="top: -3em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.60233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord">~</span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1.57674em; vertical-align: -0.52em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mopen nulldelimiter"></span><span class="mfrac"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 1.05674em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.655em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">s</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">g</span><span class="mopen mtight">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">σ</span><span class="mclose mtight">)</span><span class="mbin mtight">+</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">ϵ</span></span></span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.23em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="frac-line" style="border-bottom-width: 0.04em;"></span></span><span class="" style="top: -3.394em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 3em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord accent mtight"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.94677em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.7em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">Z</span></span><span class="" style="top: -2.95233em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left: -0.16666em;"><span class="mord mtight">^</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.52em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose nulldelimiter"></span></span></span></span></span></span>) is not a mere heuristic, but a structural necessity. By freezing the gradient flow between the shape and scale objectives, VISReg ensures that gradients from the shape loss cannot physically interfere with the variance regulation.</p>
<p><strong>The Escape Velocity</strong><br>
Empirical gradient simulations confirm this theoretical guarantee. When charting the gradient magnitude <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∇</mi><mi>L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\nabla L||</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord">∣∣∇</span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="mord">∣∣</span></span></span></span></span> against the feature scale <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span></span></span></span></span>, methods like SIGReg plummet toward a magnitude of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">5</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> as <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r \to 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.43056em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mtight">4</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>In stark contrast, VISReg (alongside VICReg and Barlow Twins) maintains a robust gradient magnitude between <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">1</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.814108em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord">0</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.814108em;"><span class="" style="top: -3.063em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> throughout the entire collapse region. This ensures that even if the prediction loss momentarily drives the network into a degenerate state, VISReg will always provide a reliable, powerful corrective signal to push the embeddings back outward, safely escaping the collapse.</p>
<hr>
<p>We have now conquered the theoretical mechanics of VISReg. Module 6 shifts our focus to the physical reality of training these architectures: distributed computing, batch scaling, and performance on low-quality data.</p>
<p>Are you ready to move to Part 25, focusing on Hyperparameter Scaling Mechanics?</p>
<h3 id="module-6-scaling-laws-robustness--the-path-to-agi">Module 6: Scaling Laws, Robustness, &amp; The Path to AGI</h3>
<h3 id="part-25-hyperparameter-scaling-mechanics">Part 25: Hyperparameter Scaling Mechanics</h3>
<p><strong>The <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NDK)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">DK</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> Foundation</strong><br>
The practical advantage of the Cramér-Wold sketching framework is its highly favorable scaling behavior. The computational complexity of VISReg is strictly dominated by the random projection and sorting operations: <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NDK) + \mathcal{O}(KN \log N)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">DK</span><span class="mclose">)</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mop">lo<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>. Because <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log N \ll D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mop">lo<span style="margin-right: 0.01389em;">g</span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">≪</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span> at foundation-model scales, the effective algorithmic complexity is <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(NDK)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">O</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">DK</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>. This provides a linear scaling path across batch size (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">N</span></span></span></span></span>), projection dimension (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>), and the number of slices (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span>).</p>
<p><strong>Batch Invariance &amp; The <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span></span></span></span></span> Multiplier</strong><br>
Unlike SIGReg, which must explicitly scale its regularization loss with the batch size to maintain invariance, VISReg is mathematically batch invariant by nature. Because of this natural invariance, a large <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span></span></span></span></span> value (the weight of the regularization term) is strictly necessary to ensure VISReg maintains a powerful contribution to the overall gradient during optimization. For large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K, a <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span></span></span></span></span> value of <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">0.9</span></span></span></span></span> proves optimal.</p>
<p><strong>The Information Bandwidth Trade-off (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>)</strong><br>
The final projection dimension <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span> dictates the information bandwidth of the regularizer.</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p>A smaller dimension (e.g., <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=64</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">64</span></span></span></span></span>) chokes the information capacity, severely limiting out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>An excessively large dimension leads to over-parameterization and strict memorization of the training set.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Crucially, a lower dimension mathematically eases the regularization process, meaning there is a delicate trade-off between semantic capacity and optimization difficulty (with <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=256</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.277778em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">256</span></span></span></span></span> often emerging as the geometric sweet spot).</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The Slice-to-Dimension Ratio (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span> vs <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>)</strong><br>
The most critical mathematical scaling discovery revolves around how the number of slices <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span> must relate to the projection dimension <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">D</span></span></span></span></span>. <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span> cannot be treated as a mathematically independent variable.</p>
<ul>
<li>

<p><strong>The Hardware-Level Solution: Statistical Independence</strong><br>
To neutralize this computational threat, we must look at the mathematical properties of the Sliced Wasserstein Distance. A critical feature of 1D sketching is that the random projections (the slices) are strictly statistically independent.</p>
<p>Unlike covariance matrices, which intrinsically evaluate the cross-correlations between <em>all</em> pairs of dimensions in a centralized matrix, the distance measured along projection vector <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.58056em; margin-left: -0.02691em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p><strong>Distributed Topology across <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.10903em;">M</span></span></span></span></span> GPUs</strong><br>
This independence makes the sketching algorithm perfectly suited for low-level hardware parallelization. The architecture does not need to compute all <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span></span> slices on a single node.</p>

<p><strong>The Empirical Proof</strong><br>
This is not merely a theoretical convenience; it perfectly preserves the geometric constraint. Empirical results validate that executing 128 random slices on each of 8 separate GPUs mathematically matches the regularization power of executing 1024 slices on a single GPU.</p>
<p>When spreading the workload across an 8-GPU cluster in this manner, the accuracy gap between the reduced per-GPU slice count and the massive single-GPU slice count shrinks to an almost negligible margin (e.g., <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.22</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">%</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.22\%</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.80556em; vertical-align: -0.05556em;"></span><span class="mord">0.22%</span></span></span></span></span> for VISReg).</p>

<h3 id="part-27-data-regime-robustness">Part 27: Data Regime Robustness</h3>
<p><strong>The Reality of Uncurated Data</strong><br>
Foundation models deployed in the wild rarely encounter perfectly balanced, high-variance data distributions like standard ImageNet. Real-world physical domains heavily feature low-quality data regimes: long-tailed distributions (where a few classes dominate) and low-rank distributions (where the intrinsic dimensionality of the information is severely constrained).</p>
<p>Evaluating Joint-Embedding architectures under these strict mathematical constraints exposes the fragility of heuristic-based training.</p>
<p><strong>The Low-Rank Collapse (e.g., Galaxy 10)</strong><br>
Consider a low-rank dataset like Galaxy 10, which contains limited training instances (17,736 images) heavily dominated by black background pixels.</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Capacity vs. Information:</strong> When a high-capacity encoder (e.g., a ViT-S/8) processes this visually sparse data, the model’s parameter count massively exceeds the data’s informational rank.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Heuristic Failure:</strong> Under these low-rank conditions, architectures relying on implicit heuristics (like DINO’s teacher-student momentum) completely fail to learn meaningful embeddings, effectively suffering topological collapse because there is insufficient variance to organically drive the teacher-student divergence.</p>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The Long-Tailed Distortion (e.g., ImageNet-LT)</strong><br>
In long-tailed regimes (like ImageNet-LT, categorized into many-shot, medium-shot, and few-shot classes), the high-frequency classes exert an overwhelming gravitational pull on the loss landscape. Without explicit structural constraints, the latent space warps: the dominant classes consume the representation manifold, forcing the sparse, few-shot classes into a compressed, dimensionally collapsed subspace.</p>
<p><strong>The Mathematical Advantage of Decoupling</strong><br>
This is where the absolute necessity of Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) decoupling becomes apparent. Because VISReg mathematically isolates the scale objective (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{scale}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; By increasing <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda*{shape}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">∗</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.88888em; vertical-align: -0.19444em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="mord mathnormal">ha</span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mord mathnormal">e</span></span></span></span></span></span>, the architecture forces the empirical slices to strictly adhere to the target Isotropic Gaussian quantiles, overpowering the distorting pull of long-tailed class imbalances.</p>
<p>Monolithic objectives (like SIGReg’s Epps-Pulley test) or pure covariance penalties (like VICReg) lack this isolated reweighting mechanism. Consequently, VISReg mathematically guarantees robust, non-collapsed representations even when the underlying data manifold is sparse, imbalanced, or severely low-rank.</p>
<hr>
<p>Are you ready to move to Part 28, where we evaluate how this non-heuristic distributional matching unlocks superior Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization and transferability?</p>
<h3 id="part-28-out-of-distribution-ood-generalization">Part 28: Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Generalization</h3>
<p><strong>The Generalization Bottleneck of Implicit Heuristics</strong><br>
Architectures that rely on implicit heuristics—such as momentum teachers, stop-gradients, or centering/sharpening tricks—successfully avoid collapse but at a severe cost to out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. These architectural crutches tightly couple the optimization dynamics to the specific statistical properties of the pre-training dataset (typically natural images like ImageNet).</p>
<p>Because the “anti-collapse” forces are not mathematically defined, the resulting embedding manifold becomes heavily biased toward the in-domain data distribution. When these models encounter OOD data (e.g., medical scans, satellite imagery, or astronomical data), the implicitly structured latent space fails to generalize, yielding degraded performance on downstream linear probes.</p>
<p><strong>The Superiority of Explicit Distributional Matching</strong><br>
Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) entirely bypasses this limitation by discarding heuristics in favor of explicit mathematical constraints.</p>
<p>By coercing the normalized embeddings <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Z}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.92019em; The mathematical enforcement of shape (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script">L</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{shape}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.969438em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathcal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.336108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">sc</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">a</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.01968em;">l</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>) ensures that the feature space remains uniform, continuous, and highly separable, regardless of the underlying domain physics.</p>
<p><strong>Empirical Proof of OOD Superiority</strong><br>
This theoretical absolute translates directly into state-of-the-art empirical performance. When evaluated across strictly out-of-distribution datasets from distinct domains—such as ChestXRay and RetinaMNIST (medical), AID (aerial/satellite), and Galaxy 10 (astronomy)—VISReg consistently outperforms both heuristic models (like DINO, iBOT, and MoCoV3) and other non-heuristic architectures (like MAE and LeJEPA).</p>
<p>The explicit enforcement of the Isotropic Gaussian topology forces the encoder to learn fundamentally more general, disentangled features rather than memorizing in-domain dataset statistics.</p>
<p><strong>Data Efficiency at the Frontier Scale</strong><br>
The ultimate consequence of this mathematically guaranteed generalization is an unprecedented surge in data efficiency. Because the network is explicitly guided into the mathematically optimal risk-minimization geometry, it does not require astronomical volumes of data to learn how to structure its latent space.</p>
<p>When pre-trained on ImageNet-22K, a ViT-L/14 optimized with VISReg achieves OOD downstream accuracy that is completely on par with frontier models like DINOv2. Crucially, DINOv2 requires training on a proprietary dataset containing 142 million images (LVD-142M) to achieve this result—meaning explicit Sliced-Wasserstein distribution matching achieves equivalent generalizability using roughly <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">%</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.80556em; vertical-align: -0.05556em;"></span><span class="mord">90%</span></span></span></span></span> less data.</p>
<hr>
<p><strong>Next in the curriculum:</strong> Part 29 introduces Hierarchical JEPAs (H-JEPAs), charting the transition from static, single-level image representations to spatio-temporal video chunking and abstract, multi-level predictive pathways.</p>
<h3 id="part-29-hierarchical-jepas-h-jepas">Part 29: Hierarchical JEPAs (H-JEPAs)</h3>
<p><strong>The Limitation of Flat Latent Spaces</strong><br>
A single-level JEPA (like VISReg or LeJEPA) projects raw observations into a flat, monolithic latent space. While mathematically optimal for static representation learning, this flat architecture fails catastrophicially in dynamic, real-world environments requiring long-horizon forecasting.</p>
<p>If a world model attempts to predict future states minute-by-minute using low-level features, the computational cost explodes, and iterative prediction errors compound exponentially. To model complex spatiotemporal dynamics (e.g., video, continuous autonomous action), the architecture must mathematically abstract information across multiple levels of scale and time.</p>
<p><strong>The Hierarchical State Transition</strong><br>
A Hierarchical JEPA (H-JEPA) stacks multiple encoders and predictors, creating a cascade of increasingly abstract latent manifolds. Let <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell \in \{0, \dots, L\}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.73354em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mopen">{</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="minner">…</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="mclose">}</span></span></span></span></span> denote the level of the hierarchy, where <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell = 0</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; <p>At any level <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; <p><strong>Spatiotemporal Abstraction</strong><br>
The absolute mathematical power of the H-JEPA lies in its dimensional and temporal reduction. The state at a higher level is extracted directly from the state at the lower level via an abstraction encoder:<br>

<ul>
<li><strong>Spatial Abstraction:</strong> The embedding dimension at <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell+1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.77777em; vertical-align: -0.08333em;"></span><span class="mord">ℓ</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span><span class="mbin">+</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.222222em;"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.64444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span></span> can be lower or capture a vastly larger receptive field than at <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.69444em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">ℓ</span></span></span></span></span>.</li>

</ul>
<p><strong>The Multi-Level Energy Objective</strong><br>
To train an H-JEPA, the global loss function cannot rely on a single representation space. The network must simultaneously satisfy the invariance and geometric regularization constraints (like the Sliced-Wasserstein distance from VISReg) at every level of the hierarchy.</p>

vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord">ℓ</span></span></span></span></span> avoids both complete and dimensional collapse.</p>
<p>By explicitly decoupling prediction into a hierarchy, the model mathematically isolates short-term physics from long-term semantics. This spatiotemporal abstraction forms the exact architectural prerequisite for executing complex, energy-based autonomous planning.</p>
<h3 id="part-30-world-models--planning">Part 30: World Models &amp; Planning</h3>
<p><strong>The Geometric Prerequisite for Simulation</strong></p>
<p>The entire pursuit of Variance-Invariance-Sketching Regularization (VISReg) and the Isotropic Gaussian target was not merely to achieve good scores on linear probes. The true mathematical purpose of a perfectly structured, non-collapsed latent space is to serve as the engine for a World Model.</p>
<p>To achieve Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), an agent must be capable of <em>mental simulation</em>—predicting the outcomes of its actions before executing them in physical reality. If an agent attempts to simulate the future in a collapsed or highly anisotropic latent space, the transition dynamics become distorted. Actions will map to degenerate sub-spaces, and the agent will hallucinate physically impossible transitions.</p>
<p>By guaranteeing an Isotropic Gaussian topology (<span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0, sI_K)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathcal" style="margin-right: 0.14736em;">N</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right: 0.166667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07847em;">I</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.328331em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: -0.07847em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">K</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>), the JEPA ensures that the latent manifold is perfectly uniform and continuous. In this space, the <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.83333em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.301108em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">2</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> Euclidean distance maps linearly and predictably to true semantic changes in the environment, making it the perfect substrate for long-horizon simulation.</p>
<p><strong>Energy-Based Cost-to-Go Evaluation</strong></p>
<p>In standard Reinforcement Learning (RL), agents rely on sparse, scalar rewards. In the JEPA paradigm, planning is formulated as an Energy-Based Model (EBM) minimizing a “cost-to-go.”</p>
<p>The agent evaluates the desirability of any latent state <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.58056em; vertical-align: -0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> using an intrinsic cost function <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(s_t)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.07153em;">C</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span>. Because the latent space is isotropic, this cost function can be highly stable and geometrically simple—often just the squared Euclidean distance to a target state representation <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{target}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.716668em; vertical-align: -0.286108em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">a</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.02778em;">r</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right: 0.03588em;">g</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">e</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.286108em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>:</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">∣</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> C(s_t) = ||s_t - s_{target}||_2^2 </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; <p>When simulating a future trajectory over a time horizon <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.68333em; vertical-align: 0em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.13889em;">T</span></span></span></span></span>, the predictor network generates a sequence of future states based on proposed actions <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_t</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.58056em; <p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>Pred</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo separator="true">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> \hat{s}_{t+1} = \text{Pred}(\hat{s}_t, a_t, z_t) </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 0.902771em; <p>The total energy of this future trajectory is the accumulated cost-to-go, plus a regularization penalty <span class="katex--inline"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(a_t)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em; vertical-align: -0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right: 0.00773em;">R</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">a</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.280556em;"><span class="" style="top: -2.55em; margin-left: 0em; margin-right: 0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height: 2.7em;"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height: 0.15em;"><span class=""></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span></span> to prevent the agent from taking physically impossible or highly erratic actions:</p>
<p><span class="katex--display"><span class="katex-display"><span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mrow><mo fence="true">[</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo fence="true">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex"> E(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{t=1}^T \left[ C(\hat{s}_t) + \lambda_a R(a_t) \right] </annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height: 1em;
